name: Framing effect
statement: Describe the same outcome as lives saved rather than lives lost and people's willingness to gamble on it reverses, though the arithmetic has not changed.
meaning: The demonstration uses two versions of one problem. A disease is expected to kill 600 people, and you choose between a certain outcome and a gamble. In the gain frame the certain option saves 200 people; in the loss frame 400 people die. Those are the same outcome stated twice. Most people take the sure thing when the choice is described in lives saved and take the gamble when it is described in deaths, which means the preference is attached to the wording rather than to the world. That is the part that matters: a preference that flips with a rephrasing cannot be a stable ranking of the outcomes themselves.

origin.note: The paper is "The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice". The reversal is explained by prospect theory, which they had published two years earlier: people are risk-averse about gains and risk-seeking about losses, so which side of the reference point a frame puts you on decides which way you lean.

evidence: Participants read one version of the problem and pick an option. In the 1981 paper 152 respondents saw the gain frame, and 72% chose the certain programme that saves 200 people. Another 155 saw the loss frame, and 22% chose the certain programme in which 400 people die, leaving 78% on the gamble. Respondents were students at Stanford University and the University of British Columbia answering brief questionnaires in class. The literature that followed is large. Kühberger pooled 136 papers reporting risky-choice framing experiments, with nearly 30,000 participants and 230 effect sizes, and concluded that framing is reliable but small to moderate, with features of the research design mattering more than the topic. Steiger and Kühberger later reanalysed that data pool using p-curve, which corrects an effect size from the distribution of significant p-values alone. Their corrected estimate was d = 0.52, against the d = 0.31 they attribute to the 1998 analysis, and they reported no evidence of intense p-hacking. A fresh meta-analysis of risk framing experiments published in 2016 gave them d = 0.56.

replication.headline: Two multi-laboratory projects re-ran two different framing scenarios from the 1981 paper, and both found the effect at roughly half the originally reported size.
replication.detail: Many Labs 1 ran the disease problem at 36 sites with 6,271 participants, substituting the country of data collection for the United States and dropping the word Asian. The unweighted estimate across sites was d = 0.62, 99% CI 0.52 to 0.71. The weighted estimate over the pooled sample was d = 0.60, 99% CI 0.53 to 0.67. Many Labs put the original at d = 1.13, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.37, computed from the cell sizes the 1981 paper reports. Consistency is worth as much as size here: 86% of the 36 samples found the effect in the same direction at p < .05, 14% found nothing, and none found it reversed. Variation between the samples was negligible, Q = 37.01 on 35 degrees of freedom, p = 0.37. Neither an American against an international sample, F = 0.09, nor laboratory against online administration, F = 1.11, moderated it. Many Labs 2 replicated Problem 10 of the same paper, where a $5 saving justifies a 20-minute drive to another branch when the discounted item is cheap but not when it is costly. That replication updated the sums for 2014 and swapped the original jacket and calculator for a ceramic vase and a wall hanging. Across 7,228 participants the odds ratio was 2.06, 95% CI 1.87 to 2.27, against 4.96, 95% CI 2.55 to 9.90, in the original 181 respondents, giving d = 0.40, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.45. Variation between samples was near zero, I-squared = 6%, 95% CI 0 to 36%, and again neither WEIRD against less WEIRD samples nor mode of administration moderated it. Whether the drop from 1.13 counts as deflation is contested. Steiger and Kühberger set their publication-bias-corrected literature estimate of d = 0.52 beside the Many Labs weighted figure of 0.60 and called the two surprisingly similar, which makes the 1981 result the outlier rather than the replications short. Two later projects tested the same material outside that laboratory network. Rachev and colleagues put the disease problem to 88,181 people in 47 countries through the COVIDiSTRESS survey between March and May 2020, again substituting the respondent's own country and dropping the word Asian. The coefficient on the frame was a log odds ratio of 1.24, standard error 0.04, which they convert to d = 0.69 and set against the Many Labs 0.60. The estimated difference is 0.08, 95% Bayesian credible interval 0.04 to 0.13, and they read the larger effect as the pandemic raising stress and risk aversion. Ruggeri and colleagues ran the 1979 prospect theory items rather than the 1981 ones, with 4,098 people in 19 countries and 13 languages. Twelve of 13 theoretical contrasts replicated, the single exception being a reflection-effect contrast, and five of the six effects held in every country, framing among them.

study.cite: Klein, R. A., Ratliff, K. A., Vianello, M., et al. (2014). Investigating variation in replicability: A "Many Labs" replication project. Social Psychology, 45(3), 142-152.

limits: What replicated is one problem, in one format, answered by people with nothing at stake. Framing is a family of effects, and the three kinds Levin, Schneider and Gaeth separated in 1998 do not behave alike. Risky-choice framing is the disease problem. Attribute framing changes how an object is judged, as when beef is 75% lean or 25% fat. Goal framing changes how persuasive a message is. Piñon and Gambara pooled 51 primary studies published between 1997 and 2003, yielding 151 effect sizes over nearly 13,500 subjects, and found d = 0.437 for risky framing, 0.260 for attribute framing and 0.444 for goal framing. That ranking is not settled. O'Keefe and Jensen reviewed 93 health-message studies covering 21,656 people and found gain-framed appeals more persuasive than loss-framed ones for disease prevention by r = .03, an advantage they trace almost wholly to messages about dental hygiene. The two meta-analyses score different quantities. Piñon and Gambara count any difference between frames; O'Keefe and Jensen count a directional advantage in persuading someone to act. A single average across the three types would bury that difference, and the replication verdict above covers risky-choice framing only. Size also varies by place. Rachev and colleagues found both the proportion of risky choices and the size of the effect varying substantially across their 47 countries, so a pooled figure hides real national spread. A neighbouring literature varies the format of a risk rather than its valence, stating the same reduction in relative or in absolute terms. Akl and colleagues' Cochrane review of 35 studies reporting 83 comparisons is recorded on this site under incomplete comparison, entry 568, and its figures are not repeated here.
misreadings: The result is often read as showing that people cannot reason about risk, which is stronger than what happened. Mandel argues the wording is doing the work. Most people read "200 will be saved" as at least 200 rather than exactly 200, and across two experiments the framing effect vanished once he made the quantifiers explicitly exact. A third experiment found that spontaneous lower-bound readings are common and strongly moderate the effect. Mandel also reports that in each of his experiments a significant majority of participants chose rationally, either maximising lives saved or answering consistently across frames. Simmons and Nelson re-ran his procedure on Mechanical Turk with about 98 people per cell against his roughly 38, and found a strong framing effect with the word exactly in place, p < .001. Their post on the blog Data Colada gives that result as a figure rather than as percentages. It reports Mandel's own Study 2 at 58% on the sure option against 26%, and at 59% against 43% once exactly was added, and notes that his preferred measure there was a continuous rating rather than the choice. The 63% against 25% that also appears in the post is Uri Simonsohn's classroom data over two years, N = 250, and not the replication. That exchange is unresolved, and it concerns what the effect means rather than whether it appears. The finding is also commonly stated as a claim about individuals, when the original and the replications measure a shift in proportions across groups. Many people give the same answer in either frame. And the disease problem gets cited as evidence for prospect theory when it was written as an illustration of it, which is a different relationship between a finding and a theory.

sources.text: Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1981). The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice. Science, 211(4481), 453-458. Problems 1 and 2 give the disease percentages; Problem 10 is the scenario Many Labs 2 replicated.

Klein, R. A., Ratliff, K. A., Vianello, M., et al. (2014). Investigating variation in replicability: A "Many Labs" replication project. Social Psychology, 45(3), 142-152. Table 2 reports unweighted and weighted estimates in separate columns; both are quoted above under their own labels.

Klein, R. A., Vianello, M., Hasselman, F., et al. (2018). Many Labs 2: Investigating variation in replicability across samples and settings. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(4), 443-490. The project ran 125 samples and 15,305 participants across 36 countries and territories, with each slate of studies given to about half of them.

Rachev, N. R., Han, H., Lacko, D., et al. (2021). Replicating the Disease framing problem during the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic: A study of stress, worry, trust, and choice under risk. PLOS ONE, 16(9), e0257151. Preregistered. The sample, the log odds ratio of 1.24 and the conversion to d = 0.69 were read from the article's JATS XML, downloaded twice with identical checksums.

Ruggeri, K., Alí, S., Berge, M. L., et al. (2020). Replicating patterns of prospect theory for decision under risk. Nature Human Behaviour, 4, 622-633. A preregistered multinational test of the 1979 prospect theory items, not of the 1981 disease problem; the contrast counts above were read from the accepted manuscript in the University of Padua repository.

Akl, E. A., Oxman, A. D., Herrin, J., et al. (2011). Using alternative statistical formats for presenting risks and risk reductions. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, (3), CD006776. Named here for the relative against absolute risk literature; its figures are given under entry 568 rather than repeated.

Kühberger, A. (1998). The influence of framing on risky decisions: A meta-analysis. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 75(1), 23-55. The counts of papers, participants and effect sizes were read from the abstract in the PubMed XML record. The pooled d = 0.31 quoted above is not in that abstract, and is read off Steiger and Kühberger's 2018 description of this analysis.
Steiger, A., & Kühberger, A. (2018). A meta-analytic re-appraisal of the framing effect. Zeitschrift für Psychologie, 226(1), 45-55.

Levin, I. P., Schneider, S. L., & Gaeth, G. J. (1998). All frames are not created equal: A typology and critical analysis of framing effects. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 76(2), 149-188.
Piñon, A., & Gambara, H. (2005). A meta-analytic review of framing effect: Risky, attribute and goal framing. Psicothema, 17(2), 325-331.

O'Keefe, D. J., & Jensen, J. D. (2007). The relative persuasiveness of gain-framed and loss-framed messages for encouraging disease prevention behaviors: A meta-analytic review. Journal of Health Communication, 12(7), 623-644.
Mandel, D. R. (2014). Do framing effects reveal irrational choice? Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 143(3), 1185-1198.

Simmons, J., & Nelson, L. (2013). "Exactly": The most famous framing effect is robust to precise wording. Data Colada, post 11, dated 19 December 2013. A blog post rather than a peer-reviewed paper, cited as the rebuttal its authors state. The whole post was read: it presents its own replication as a chart and prints no percentages for it, and the 63% and 25% it does print belong to the classroom data it attributes to Uri Simonsohn.
